title: There is / exists: байна, байгаа, байдаг
summary: All three come from the verb 'to be'. Байна states something true right now (or very soon), typically something you can see or point to. Байгаа also states something true right now, but something not currently visible to the speaker — still real, just not in view. Байдаг states something habitually or generally true, not tied to this moment. Negatives: байхгүй (no ... right now / not visible), байдаггүй (not generally the case).
sourceCite: Nomiin Ger — Beginner Mongolian Part 1, Lesson 5 (p.48-50)

examples.en: The milk is on the table (right now, in view).
The book is at home (right now, though not in view).
We have a cat at home (as a rule, generally).

drills.prompt: Ном ширээн дээр ___. (right now — you can see it)
Манай байшинд муур ___. (we generally keep one)
Цахилгаан ___. (there is no electricity right now)

drills.fromEn: The milk is on the table.
drills.toEn: The milk is NOT on the table.

drills.en: We keep a cat at home (generally).

title: Question particles (уу / юу / бэ / вэ)
summary: A yes/no question adds a particle to the end of a statement, the way a question mark does in English. уу/үү (or юу/юү after a long vowel) turn a statement into a yes/no question — which one depends on vowel harmony. A wh-question (who, what, where) instead adds бэ after a word ending in м, н or в, and вэ after anything else.
sourceCite: Nomiin Ger — Beginner Mongolian Part 1, Lesson 1 (p.2-5)

drills.hint: add -уу to turn a statement into a yes/no question

title: Having and lacking: -тай / -тэй / -той, and -гүй
summary: Adding -тай (-тэй, -той by vowel harmony: а/у → -тай, э/и/ө/ү → -тэй, о/ё → -той) to a noun means 'have' or 'with'. -гүй, unchanged by harmony, is the opposite: 'lack' or 'without'. Compare this to байна/байгаа: -тай marks something more lasting or defining (Би машинтай — I own a car), while байна/байгаа marks having something right now, not necessarily for good (Надад машин байгаа — I have a car, for now).
sourceCite: Nomiin Ger — Beginner Mongolian Part 1, Lesson 2 (p.11-14)

drills.prompt: сүү (milk) + with → сүү___ цай (tea with milk)

title: Marking the object: -ыг / -ийг
summary: The direct object of a sentence can take -ыг (after back-vowel words), -ийг (after front-vowel words, and back-vowel words ending in ж/ч/ш/г/ь/и), or just -г (after a long vowel). It marks a specific, known object — 'the book', not 'a book' — and is often dropped when the object is general or indefinite. 'Би ном уншина' (I'll read a book/books) and 'Би номыг уншина' (I'll read the book) are both grammatical; the ending is what tells them apart.
sourceCite: Modern Mongolian: A course book (Gaunt & Bayarmandakh), Chapter One p.5-6

examples.en: I'll read a book (some book, unspecified).
He/she will read that book (a specific one).

drills.prompt: Хоол___ идье. (Let's eat the food — a specific plate of it)
Which means 'He reads a book' (some book, not a specific one)?

drills.hint: add -ыг once the book is one specific, known book

title: Habitual present: -даг / -дэг / -дог / -дөг
summary: Added to a verb stem, this ending states something done habitually, regularly, or as a matter of routine — not just today. 'Би ном уншдаг' is 'I read books' in the sense of a habit or an occupation, not a description of what is happening right now. English 'usually' or 'often' is often implied rather than translated. The vowel changes by harmony, the same four-way pattern as -тай/-тэй/-той/-той in the previous topic.
sourceCite: Modern Mongolian: A course book (Gaunt & Bayarmandakh), Chapter Four p.35-38

examples.en: I drink tea in the morning (habitually).

drills.prompt: Which means 'I read books' (as a habit)?

drills.fromEn: I drink tea in the morning (habitually).
drills.toEn: I am drinking tea right now.
